solution:
Domestic trade (internal trade).

Maharashtra and Punjab are two regions within the same country, and the chapter says that domestic or internal trade takes place between different regions within the same country.

International trade (external trade), and since it takes place between two countries, it is bilateral trade.

India and Japan are two different countries, and the chapter says that international trade means the exchange of goods and services of one country with other countries, and that international trade between two countries is bilateral trade.

Domestic trade (internal trade), at the local or regional level.

Lasalgaon and Pune are both places within the same country, in fact within the same state of Maharashtra, so the trade between them is trade between different regions within the same country. The chapter says that on the basis of the extent of the region, trade can be divided into local, regional, national and international trade.

International trade (external trade), and since it takes place between two countries, it is bilateral trade.

China and Canada are two different countries, so the exchange of goods and services between them is international trade, and the chapter says that international trade between two countries is called bilateral trade.

International trade (external trade), and since it takes place between more than two countries, it is multilateral trade.

The European Union is an organisation of 28 member nations in Europe, so trade between India and the European Union is trade between India and many countries together. The chapter says that when international trade occurs between more than two countries it is called multilateral trade.

Import.

Crude oil is scarce in India and India buys it from other countries. The chapter says that when a country buys those goods and services which are scarce in their own country from another country, it is known as import.

Export.

Canada produces wheat in excess of its own need and sells it to Asian countries which have a demand for it. The chapter says that when a country produces excess goods or services than required and sells these to countries which have a demand for it, it is called export.

Export.

Japan sends its own machine parts out to the APEC countries which have a demand for them, and the chapter says that selling excess goods produced in a country to countries which have a demand for them is called export.

This statement is wrong.

Corrected statement: India is not a self-sufficient country.

The chapter says that the economic life of people is interdependent and that no region or country is self-sufficient. Each region has different geographical conditions, so each region produces only specific commodities, and trade between regions is necessary to fulfil the needs of the people.

This statement is correct, so it does not need to be rewritten.

The chapter says that there is demand for a commodity at the place where there is a paucity of it, while the place where it is abundant provides the supply of that commodity. So supply is done from regions producing excess commodities to regions facing a deficit, according to the demand. For example, apples produced in Jammu and Kashmir are sent to other states of India having a demand for them.

This statement is wrong.

Corrected statement: International trade processes are more complex than local trade.

The chapter says that carrying out trade at an international level is a more complex process than domestic trade, because trade takes place between two or more nations and factors like the economy of the country, government policies, markets, laws, judicial system, currency and language influence it. The political relations between the two countries also influence the trade between them.

This statement is wrong.

Corrected statement: ASEAN works towards economic development and enhancing the social and cultural harmony of the South-East Asian countries.

The chapter's table of economic organisations gives expanding social and cultural harmony along with economic growth in South-East Asia as an aim of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN), whose headquarters is at Jakarta in Indonesia. SAARC is the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, so it works for the South Asian countries and not the South-East Asian countries. Its aims are to find satisfactory solutions to the common problems faced by countries in South Asia, to increase social welfare, raise the living standard and increase regional cooperation among member states, and to remove unrest in South Asia.

Retail trade.

Srushti is a consumer and she has bought a small quantity of sugar from a grocery shop. The chapter says that when traders buy goods from wholesale traders and sell them directly to consumers it is known as retail trading, and that the quantity of goods sold in this case is less.

Wholesale trade.

The traders have bought cotton on a large scale directly from the farmers, who are the producers. The chapter says that when traders buy commodities on a large scale directly from the producers it is called wholesale trading, and that wholesale traders buy goods on a large scale from industrialists, farmers and others.

International trade (external trade), and it is the export part of that trade.

Sameer has sent his pomegranates from India to Australia, that is from one country to another country. The chapter says that international trade means the exchange of goods and services of one country with other countries, and that selling goods to a country which has a demand for them is called export.

Retail trade.

Sadabhau has bought the wheat and rice from the Market Yard, that is from the wholesale market, and he will sell it in his own shop directly to consumers in small quantities. The chapter says that when traders buy goods from wholesale traders and sell them directly to consumers, it is known as retail trading.

The chapter classifies trade on two bases, and each basis has two types:

| Basis of the classification | Types of trade |
|---|---|
| On the basis of the quantity of goods | Wholesale trade, Retail trade |
| On the basis of the extent of the trade region | Domestic (internal) trade, International (external) trade |

In the flowchart, 'Types of trade' is written in the top box. Two arrows go down from it, one to 'on the basis of the quantity of goods' and the other to 'on the basis of the extent of the trade region'. From the first branch, two arrows lead to 'Wholesale trade' and 'Retail trade'. From the second branch, two arrows lead to 'Domestic or internal trade' and 'International or external trade'.

The chapter also mentions that on the basis of the extent of the region trade can be divided into local, regional, national and international trade, and that buying and selling of goods is called visible trade while an exchange of services is called invisible trade.

The difference between the import and export values of a country in a specific period is called the balance of trade. The chapter gives three types of it.

| Type of balance of trade | When it occurs |
|---|---|
| Unfavourable balance of trade | When the value of imports is more than the value of exports |
| Favourable balance of trade | When the value of exports is more than the value of imports |
| Balanced balance of trade | When the value of exports and imports is almost the same |

So the three types differ only in which side of the trade is greater. A country that buys more from other countries than it sells has an unfavourable balance of trade, a country that sells more than it buys has a favourable balance of trade, and a country whose buying and selling are nearly equal in value has a balanced balance of trade.

The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has 164 member states and its headquarters is at Geneva in Switzerland. Its objectives are:

- To provide a platform for negotiations in international trade.
- To handle the differences related to trade.
- To monitor the trade policies of member states.
- To provide technological assistance and training to developing countries.

OPEC and APEC differ in what they deal with. OPEC works with one commodity, crude oil, while APEC works with the general trade and economy of one region.

| Point | OPEC | APEC |
|---|---|---|
| Full form | Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries | Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation |
| Members | 13 | 21 |
| Headquarters | Vienna (Austria) | Singapore |
| Functions | Controlling the international trade of crude oil; controlling the rates of crude oil production among member states; maintaining consensus in oil export | Free trade and economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Ocean region; promoting regional and technical cooperation among members |

Thus OPEC controls the trade, the production rates and the export of crude oil among its members, while APEC works for free trade and for economic, regional and technical cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Ocean region.

The chapter's table gives three important trade organisations working in Asia, SAARC, ASEAN and APEC.

| Organisation | Members | Headquarters | Functions |
|---|---|---|---|
| South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) | 8 | Kathmandu (Nepal) | Finding satisfactory solutions to the common problems faced by countries in South Asia; increasing social welfare, raising the living standard and increasing regional cooperation among member states; removing unrest in South Asia |
| Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) | 10 | Jakarta (Indonesia) | Expanding social and cultural harmony along with economic growth in South-East Asia; promoting regional peace; promoting tax waivers for trade growth in member states |
| Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) | 21 | Singapore | Free trade and economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Ocean region; promoting regional and technical cooperation among members |

The headquarters of BRICS, the organisation of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, is also in Asia, at Shanghai in China. It makes funds available for the growth of the economies of its 5 members, enhances mutual economic cooperation and strengthens economic security.

Marketing is very important for a farmer because the price of a commodity is determined by its quality, its grading and the way it is presented before the customer. The chapter tells us about Dhondiba, who grew the best varieties of vegetables and other agricultural commodities with a lot of hard work but whose products could not fetch a good price. His son cleaned the commodities neatly, packed them nicely and contacted the supermarket in the town, which advertised the farm product and kept it for sale in the mall, and after that Dhondiba's commodities began to be sold at higher prices than before. So through marketing a farmer's produce reaches a large number of consumers, the whole production can be distributed at once on a large scale, the selling price of the product increases and the demand for the product also increases. This is why proper cleaning, grading, packaging, advertisement and distribution are necessary for agricultural products.

The compound bar graph:

Take the four countries, China, India, Brazil and USA, along the X-axis and the value of trade in million U.S. dollars along the Y-axis. As the largest figure is 2380, a scale such as 1 cm = 200 million U.S. dollars, with the Y-axis marked from 0 up to 2400, is suitable. For each country draw two bars of equal width side by side, one for the export value and one for the import value, and shade the two bars differently. Show the meaning of the two shades in an index, as is done in the figures of favourable, unfavourable and balanced trade in this chapter. The bars for China will be 2143 and 1960 units high, for India 272 and 380, for Brazil 190 and 241, and for USA 1510 and 2380.

What the graph shows:

For China the export bar is taller than the import bar. For India, Brazil and the USA the import bar is taller than the export bar. The bars of China and the USA are far taller than those of India and Brazil, so these two countries carry on trade of a much larger value.

Balance of trade of each country:

| Country | Export | Import | Difference | Type of balance of trade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| China | 2143 | 1960 | Exports more by 183 | Favourable balance of trade |
| India | 272 | 380 | Imports more by 108 | Unfavourable balance of trade |
| Brazil | 190 | 241 | Imports more by 51 | Unfavourable balance of trade |
| USA | 1510 | 2380 | Imports more by 870 | Unfavourable balance of trade |

Comment: Only China has a favourable balance of trade, because the value of its exports is more than the value of its imports. India, Brazil and the USA all have an unfavourable balance of trade, because the value of their imports is more than the value of their exports. Among these three the USA has the largest gap of 870 million U.S. dollars, and Brazil the smallest of 51 million U.S. dollars. None of the four countries has a balanced balance of trade, as in no case are the export and import values almost the same.

[Note: the chapter does not define 'balance of payments'. It defines only the balance of trade, which is the difference between the import and export values of a country in a specific period, and the comment above has been made using that term and the chapter's own types of balance of trade.]
